strengths: First-order-optimal (in T) convergence guarantee for nonconvex decentralized stochastic optimization under heavy-tailed noise with only a finite p-th moment (p ∈ (1,2]), matching the centralized lower bound — a meaningful open problem that prior decentralized works [29, 30] addressed only under strong convexity, compact domains, or symmetry assumptions.

The algorithm design is well-motivated: the paper includes an instructive negative result (Claim 1, with proof) showing vanilla decentralized normalization can stay arbitrarily far from the optimum under heterogeneity, which clarifies why gradient tracking plus momentum variance reduction is necessary.

Both a rate for known tail index p (order-optimal O(1/T^{(p-1)/(3p-2)})) and a parameter-free version when p is unknown (O(1/T^{(p-1)/(2p)})), the latter matching best-known centralized rates and being topology-independent with an n^{1-1/p} speedup — practically relevant results.

Experimental evaluation covers multiple noise types (Gaussian, Student's t, Lévy α-stable), three graph topologies, ablations over λ, σ, and n, and a real-world decentralized Transformer (GPT, 3M parameters on Multi30k) training task where the method dramatically outperforms baselines; hyperparameter grids are reported in detail, aiding reproducibility.
Related work is thorough and positions the contribution clearly against centralized clipping/normalization methods, server-based distributed methods, and existing decentralized nonlinear methods.
weaknesses: The appendix proofs contain numerous typos and apparent errors that undermine confidence in full rigor without a careful check: e.g., inconsistent notation (ξ^{t,b}, ∇gi(x,ξ), mismatched indices such as ∥gi(x^k_i,ξ^k_i)−∇fi(x^k)∥ in Lemma 8's derivation, y_0^i = 0 vs ȳ_0 in the recursion of Lemma 6), and several multi-line derivations (Lemmas 6–8, steps (i)–(iii) on pages 19–22) are compressed and hard to verify; the chain in the proof of Lemma 8 seems to swap summation order without justification.

The claimed constant-factor and n-dependence details are hard to audit: the final bounds carry many terms with different powers of n (e.g., σ n^{1/2}/((1−λ)^{1/p} T^{p/(3p−2)}) in Theorem 1), and Remarks 5–6 rely on asymptotic dominance arguments for 'sufficiently large T' that are not quantified; the actual regime in which the n^{1-1/p} speedup holds is unclear.

The stepsize α and momentum 1−β in Theorem 1 require knowledge of problem-dependent quantities (Δ0, L, λ, T) and of the tail index p, limiting practical applicability; no parameter-free or adaptive variant is analyzed or tested against the theoretically prescribed schedules in the experiments.

Normalization by ∥y^t_r∥ is undefined when the tracker y^t_i = 0; the paper does not discuss whether such events can occur (e.g., at exact stationary points or early iterations) or how they are handled in theory and practice.

Experiments are modest in scale: the 'real-world' evaluation is a 3M-parameter GPT on the small Multi30k dataset; on the synthetic task GT-NSGDm is actually outperformed by the SClip-EF-Network baseline (acknowledged but a weakness), and no comparison with centralized or server-based heavy-tail methods (e.g., TailOPT-style) is provided.
The results are in-expectation only; high-probability guarantees, which are available for several centralized heavy-tail baselines, are not addressed.

strengths: Addresses an underexplored and practically relevant problem: decentralized nonconvex optimization under heavy-tailed gradient noise, where prior work [29, 30] required strong convexity, compact domains, or noise symmetry.

Provides the first in-expectation convergence guarantee with an explicit rate O(1/T^{(p-1)/(3p-2)}) for this setting, matching the centralized lower bound of [17], and a second result for unknown tail index p that is topology-independent with an n^{1-1/p} speedup.

Claim 1 (vanilla decentralized normalization can stall arbitrarily far from optimality) is a nice negative result that motivates the algorithm design and gives insight into why gradient tracking plus momentum is necessary.

Experiments cover both controlled synthetic noise injections and real decentralized Transformer training across three graph topologies, with reasonable baselines (DSGD, DSGD-Clip, GT-DSGD, SClip-EF-Network) and grid-search tuning for all methods.
The proof structure (descent lemma on network average, consensus error bounds, martingale moment bounds) is coherent and the main lemmas are, at a high level, correct.
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: GT-NSGDm is a fairly direct composition of known components — normalization from centralized heavy-tailed SGD [26, 27], gradient tracking [12, 13], and momentum/error-feedback from [30]. The main contribution is the analysis, not the method; the paper would benefit from more discussion of what is genuinely new beyond transplanting [27]'s techniques into a decentralized proof template.

The 'optimal convergence' claim is relative to the centralized lower bound of [17]. No decentralized lower bound is established, so the dependence on λ and n (e.g., the 1/(1-λ) and n^{1/2} terms in the bound, and the conditions needed for the claimed speedup regime in Remark 5) may well be suboptimal. The optimality language is stronger than the evidence.

A theory-practice gap: the stepsize α in (5) requires knowledge of Δ0, L, and λ, and the momentum schedule 1-β = T^{-p/(3p-2)} requires knowing T and p — yet in the experiments all hyperparameters are set by grid search, and the Transformer runs use small, fixed grids. The practical algorithm differs from the analyzed one, and no experiment validates the theoretical parameter choices.

The proofs contain several errors and typos that undermine confidence: Lemma 3 asserts ∥x̄^{t+1} - x̄^t∥ = α∥ỹ^t∥ = α, which is incorrect (only ≤ α holds since ∥ỹ^t∥ ≤ 1); Lemma 8's derivation has index inconsistencies (x^t vs. x^k, ξ_{t,b}) and a malformed term '∇gi(x^t_i, ξ^t_i) - fi(x̄^k)'; several 'recursively applying' steps in Lemmas 6-8 are asserted rather than shown; the proof of Claim 1 mislabels x^0_r vs. x^0_i.

Experimental scale is modest: the synthetic task is d=20 with 1k samples, and the Transformer is only 3M parameters on Multi30k. On the synthetic task the proposed method is actually outperformed by SClip-EF-Network; the claimed advantage rests mainly on one small-scale LM experiment. Missing comparisons with recent server-based heavy-tail methods [23, 35, 44] (even acknowledging the different setting) and no ablation isolating the contribution of momentum vs. gradient tracking.

The constant-heavy final bounds in Theorems 1-2 are difficult to interpret, and the 'dominant term' analysis justifying Remarks 5 and 6 requires T to be 'sufficiently large' in a way that is never quantified; the empirical speedup in n (Figure 3c) shows a plateau at n=40, only loosely supporting the n^{1-1/p} theory.

Writing quality issues: typos ('exits' for 'exists', 'over over random quantities'), a garbled Remark 7 referencing undefined ε, and dense theorem statements that obscure which terms actually control the rate.

strengths: Clear and significant theoretical contribution: GT-NSGDm achieves the optimal iteration complexity O(1/T^((p-1)/(3p-2))) for decentralized nonconvex optimization under heavy-tailed noise with only a finite p-th moment (p in (1,2]), matching the centralized lower bound; this is claimed and appears to be the first such optimal result in the decentralized setting.

The assumptions are notably weaker than prior decentralized work ([29],[30]): no compact domain, no strong convexity, no symmetry of the noise, and only a p-th central moment condition — making the results relevant to modern deep learning where gradient noise is heavy-tailed and possibly has infinite variance.

The paper includes a valuable negative result (Claim 1 and Remark 3) showing that vanilla normalization in decentralized SGD can leave iterates arbitrarily far from the optimum due to heterogeneous local gradient norms. This cleanly motivates the joint design of gradient tracking + momentum variance reduction + normalization, and strengthens the paper beyond a straightforward extension of centralized analyses.
The algorithm handles the topology-independent (in the leading term) rate for unknown tail index p (Theorem 2), with an explicit n^{1-1/p} speedup, which is a practically meaningful refinement.

The proofs in the appendix are reasonably self-contained and structured (consensus error, gradient estimation error, martingale bounds via a vector-valued Bernstein-type lemma), and the main proof steps I traced appear correct.

Experiments cover both controlled synthetic settings (three noise types, three topologies, ablations over λ, σ, n) and a real-world task (decentralized GPT training on Multi30k over three graph topologies with 5 seeds and std reported), with sensible baselines (DSDG, DSGD-Clip, GT-DSDG, SClip-EF-Network) and grid-searched hyperparameters. The results support the robustness claims, and the n-dependence study qualitatively supports the theoretical speedup.
weaknesses: The optimality claim is relative to the centralized lower bound [17]; no decentralized-specific lower bound is provided, so it remains possible that the 1/(1-λ) dependence in the non-leading terms of Theorem 1 (and the requirement of sufficiently large T for the topology-independent claim in Theorem 2) is suboptimal. The topology-independence claim for unknown p holds only for the asymptotically leading terms.

The results are in-expectation only; given the heavy-tailed setting, high-probability guarantees (available in some centralized and server-based works, e.g., [44]) would be stronger, and their absence narrows the gap to related work in terms of guarantee type.

The stepsize choice (5) depends on unknown problem parameters (Δ0, L, σ, λ), so the theoretically optimal rates are not directly implementable; experiments rely on grid search. A parameter-free or adaptive variant would significantly strengthen practical relevance.

The empirical n-speedup evidence (Figure 3c) is limited: final errors [0.4, 0.35, 0.29, 0.20, 0.21] show improvement only over a range of n and flatten at n=40, providing only weak qualitative support for the n^{1-1/p} factor.

The Transformer experiments use a small model (3M parameters) and a single dataset; the claimed advantage over SClip-EF-Network is small in the synthetic low-dimensional setting, so the practical superiority over the strongest baseline rests on a fairly narrow empirical base. Also, the theory measures gradient-norm stationarity while experiments measure loss/perplexity, which is standard but an indirect match.

Some technical presentation issues: the stepsize formula min(1, max(·,·,·)) in (5) is unusual and its correctness in simultaneously satisfying all constraints used in the proof is not separately verified; the assumption β ≥ 1/10 appears ad hoc; several constants (e.g., the 2√2 factors) suggest the bounds are loose in constants.
The momentum design requires β → 1 at a specific rate tied to p (or 1/√T when p is unknown), which is a nonstandard tuning requirement not validated through sensitivity analysis in the experiments.

strengths: Clear and meaningful theoretical contribution: the paper is, to the authors' credible knowledge, the first to establish an order-optimal in-expectation convergence rate O(1/T^{(p-1)/(3p-2)}) for decentralized nonconvex smooth optimization under heavy-tailed gradient noise with only a bounded p-th moment (p in (1,2)), matching the best-known centralized lower bound; this relaxes strong convexity, compactness/bounded-gradient, and symmetry assumptions in prior decentralized works [29,30].

Two complementary guarantees: an optimal rate when the tail index p is known (Theorem 1) and a p-free rate O(1/T^{(p-1)/(2p)}) when p is unknown (Theorem 2), with topology-independent asymptotic behavior and a clean n^{-1/p} speedup in the number of nodes — a practically relevant and non-trivial analysis outcome.

The paper motivates the algorithm design well: the negative result (Claim 1) showing that vanilla decentralized normalization can keep iterates arbitrarily far from optimality is simple, convincing, and gives real insight into why gradient tracking plus momentum is needed, rather than being an ad hoc combination.

Complete proofs are included (Appendix B), with a transparent proof structure (consensus error and gradient estimation error lemmas, martingale moment bounds), and the analysis carefully handles the nonlinearity introduced by normalization interacting with the mixing matrix — the technical crux of the problem.

Experiments cover both controlled synthetic heavy-tail noise (Gaussian, Student's t, Lévy α-stable) and a decentralized GPT training task on Multi30k, across three graph topologies, with a reasonable set of theory-backed and practical baselines, ablations on λ, σ, and n, and honest reporting (e.g., acknowledging that DSGD-GClip slightly outperforms and lacks theory, and that decentralized training is simulated).
Hyperparameter search grids, baseline descriptions, and hardware details are provided, supporting reproducibility of the experimental claims.
weaknesses: The algorithm is a combination of known ingredients: normalization for heavy-tailed noise from the centralized literature [26,27], gradient tracking [12,13], and momentum/error-feedback variance reduction [30]. The novelty is primarily in the analysis achieving the optimal rate in the decentralized setting rather than in algorithmic design; the paper would benefit from a sharper articulation of what is technically new beyond adapting [27]'s analysis.

The noise model assumes zero-mean noise with a bounded p-th moment; recent works [28,42,43] handle nonzero-mean noise with only a first absolute moment (albeit with weaker/slower or non-explicit rates), so the setting is not uniformly the most general — the positioning against this line could be more careful, and a discussion of high-probability guarantees (absent here) is warranted.

The 'optimal' claim hinges on matching the lower bound of [17], which is derived for the centralized setting; the paper does not prove a decentralized-specific lower bound, so optimality claims for the decentralized problem class (e.g., unavoidable dependence on λ) are not fully established.

The speedup in n is conditional: it appears only in the high-noise regime, requires sufficiently large T (small target gap), and the constants carry potentially large 1/(1-λ) factors; Remark 8 concedes the speedup vanishes as p → 1. The empirical evidence for the n^{-1/p} speedup (Figure 3(c)) is qualitative only, with no rate-fitting against the theory.

Experimental scale is modest: the Transformer is only 3M parameters trained on a small corpus, decentralized training is simulated on a single GPU, and the synthetic task is 20-dimensional regression; the empirically best baseline (DSGD-GClip) slightly beats GT-NSGDM on all three topologies, which slightly weakens the practical case for the added complexity of momentum and gradient tracking.

Hyperparameter selection in Theorem 1 requires knowledge of Δ0, L, λ, n, and p (for the momentum schedule 1-β = T^{-(p-2)/(3p-2)}), and β ≥ 1/10 is assumed; Remark 7 partially addresses this, but the gap between theory-recommended and grid-searched parameters used in the experiments is not discussed.

Several constant-level steps in the proofs (e.g., repeated Jensen/Minkowski relaxations in Lemmas 6–8) suggest the bounds may be loose in the dependence on n and (1-λ), which the authors partially acknowledge; a tighter analysis or empirical verification of the predicted parameter dependence (beyond trends) would strengthen the contribution.

strengths: Clear and meaningful theoretical contribution: the paper establishes, for the first time, an order-optimal in-expectation rate O(1/T^{(p-1)/(3p-2)}) for decentralized nonconvex optimization under heavy-tailed (finite p-th moment, p ∈ (1,2)) gradient noise, matching the centralized lower bound, under relatively mild assumptions (no compact domain, bounded gradients, or symmetry), which clearly improves over prior decentralized works [29,30] that required strong convexity and restrictive assumptions.

The unknown-p result (Theorem 2), achieving the best-known centralized rate without knowledge of the tail index and with a topology-independent n^{-1/p} speedup for large T, is a useful practical extension, and the hyperparameter-selection discussion (Remark 7) partially addresses the dependence on λ.

The paper includes a valuable negative result (Claim 1 and Remark 3) showing that vanilla decentralized normalized GD can stall arbitrarily far from optimality, which motivates the algorithm design (normalization applied only to the gradient tracker) and adds insight beyond a pure upper-bound result.

The proofs in the appendix are detailed and structured (descent lemma, consensus error bounds, martingale moment bounds via a vector-valued Bernstein-type lemma), and appear technically sound at the level verifiable from the manuscript.

Experiments cover both a controlled synthetic setting with injected Gaussian/Student-t/Lévy noise and decentralized GPT training, include several topology variants and ablations on λ, σ, and n, and report hyperparameter grids for all baselines; the paper is transparent that the best-performing empirical baseline (DSGD-GClip) lacks theoretical guarantees.
The writing is generally clear, with a well-organized related-work section that carefully positions the contribution relative to centralized adaptive-methods theory and distributed nonlinear methods.
weaknesses: Algorithmic novelty is limited: GT-NSGDm is essentially a combination of known ingredients — gradient normalization from centralized heavy-tail work [26,27], momentum/error-feedback variance reduction from [30], and standard gradient tracking [12,13]. The main novelty lies in the analysis, which is legitimate but narrows the conceptual contribution.

There is a likely error or at least a serious typo in Theorem 1's parameter selection: as written, 1 − β = 1/T^{(p−2)/(3p−2)}. For p ∈ (1,2) the exponent (p−2)/(3p−2) is negative, so 1 − β = T^{(2−p)/(3p−2)} > 1, contradicting β ∈ (0,1) and the assumption β ≥ 1/10. The intended statement is presumably β = 1 − T^{−(2−p)/(3p−2)}, and the final rate derivation suggests this is what the proof uses, but as stated the theorem is internally inconsistent and must be corrected/clarified.

All guarantees are in-expectation only; no high-probability results are provided, whereas competing lines of work under heavy-tailed noise often provide high-probability bounds. Additionally, the noise is still required to be zero-mean, so the claimed relaxation relative to [30] (symmetry) is only partial.

Practical applicability of the theory is limited: in the 'known p' regime the step size α in (5) depends on the unknown noise scale σ (and λ), and the rate in the unknown-p regime requires β ≥ 1/10 conditions; the gap between theory and the hyperparameter grids actually used in experiments is not discussed.

Empirical evidence is modest in scale and realism: the synthetic problem is d = 20 linear regression, and the Transformer experiment is a 3M-parameter GPT trained on a simulated 8-node decentralized setup on a single GPU. The proposed method does not outperform the best empirical baseline (DSGD-GClip: 0.253 vs. 0.258–0.282), so the experiments support robustness claims but not a clear practical advantage.

The theoretically guaranteed baselines (DSGD-Clip, SClip-EF-Network) perform near chance level (≈5.6 validation loss) in Table 1, which may indicate insufficient tuning rather than algorithmic inferiority; the paper does not analyze this discrepancy.

Several important proof steps (e.g., the step from (35)(ii) to (35)(iii), where α in (36) is substituted) are compressed and hard to verify; given the hyperparameter inconsistency noted above, an independent end-to-end verification of the exponents in Theorems 1–2 is warranted.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem: decentralized nonconvex optimization under heavy-tailed gradient noise is underexplored, and the paper identifies genuine technical obstacles (nonlinearity of normalization interacting with peer-to-peer averaging).

Main theoretical result is significant: GT-NSGDm achieves the order-optimal in-expectation rate O(1/T^{(p-1)/(3p-2)}) for general smooth nonconvex objectives, matching the centralized lower bound, and relaxes restrictive assumptions of prior decentralized works [29, 30] (no compact domain, no strong convexity, no noise symmetry).

The result for unknown tail index p with a topology-independent rate and an explicit n^{1-1/p} linear speedup is a nice, practically relevant refinement, with a careful discussion of hyperparameter selection and when dependence on λ can be removed.

The paper includes a negative result (Claim 1) showing vanilla decentralized normalization can stall arbitrarily far from optimum, which convincingly justifies the gradient-tracking-plus-momentum design and elevates the contribution beyond a straightforward combination of existing ideas.

The analysis is self-contained and appears technically careful: a clean descent-lemma recursion coupled with consensus-error and gradient-estimation-error bounds, with proofs included in the appendix.

Experiments are reasonably thorough for the claims made: three noise types, three graph topologies, controlled studies of dependence on λ, σ, and n that qualitatively match the theory, plus a decentralized GPT training experiment with several baselines and hyperparameter grids documented.
weaknesses: All guarantees are in-expectation bounds on the ℓ2 norm of the gradient; no high-probability results are provided, whereas some related work (e.g., [44]) obtains high-probability guarantees in distributed heavy-tailed settings. This weakens the practical relevance for heavy-tailed noise, where expectation bounds can mask instability.

The optimal rate requires knowledge of the tail index p to set 1-β = 1/T^{(3p-2)/(3p-2)}; the unknown-p result has a strictly slower rate O(1/T^{(p-1)/(2p)}), and the assumption β ≥ 1/10 is a somewhat ad hoc technical restriction.

Experiments are relatively small scale: the Transformer experiment uses a 3M-parameter GPT model simulated on a single GPU over Multi30k, and on it GT-NSGDm is slightly outperformed by DSGD-GClip, which has no theoretical guarantee under heavy-tailed noise. This leaves open the question of whether the theoretically optimal method is also the best practical choice.

The convergence measure is averaged over all iterates and nodes of E[||∇f(x_i^t)||], including the consensus-related bias term αλL/(1-λ) that does not vanish with T; while standard, this makes the 'optimal rate' claim somewhat less clean than in the centralized setting.

The central contribution is largely an adaptation of the centralized normalized-SGD analysis of [26, 27] to the decentralized setting via gradient tracking; the proof techniques (descent lemma, consensus error decomposition, martingale moment bounds) are standard in the decentralized literature, so the methodological novelty is moderate.

Some empirical claims are only weakly supported: the speedup in n (Figure 3c) shows only marginal improvements over certain n ranges, and the empirical evidence for heavy tails (Figure 1) is a small visual comparison rather than formal tail-index estimation.

Several steps in the analysis use tuned constants (e.g., the 3.5 factor in the stepsize and bound), and the O(·) statements preserve all problem parameters, making the theorems dense and hard to parse; a cleaner statement separating the T-, n-, and λ-dependence would improve readability.
